title: Kantor v. Commissioner
court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
subject: Section 174 Research Expenditures
summary: Kantor v. Commissioner, 998 F.2d 1514 (9th Cir. 1993), governs when pre-operational partnerships and R&D syndicates may deduct research and experimental expenditures under I.R.C. § 174(a)(1) in the United States. The Ninth Circuit held that a taxpayer funding contract research must show a realistic prospect—both objective intent and capability—of entering its own trade or business using the technology.

body.text: (1) Executive Summary & Case Background
Procedural Posture and the Taxpayer's Claim

In Kantor v. Commissioner, 998 F.2d 1514 (9th Cir. 1993), affirming in part and reversing in part T.C. Memo. 1990-380, 60 T.C.M. (CCH) 225 (1990), the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit established the controlling appellate standard for determining when a pre-operational entity or research syndicate incurs research and experimental (R&E) expenditures "in connection with [its] trade or business" under Internal Revenue Code (I.R.C.) § 174(a)(1). The litigation arose from the 1981 federal income tax return of petitioners-appellants Robert E. Kantor and Sharon D. Kantor, who claimed a pass-through distributive share deduction for research and experimental losses generated by PCS, Ltd., a limited partnership in which they held limited partnership interests. Under fundamental principles of United States partnership taxation codified in Subchapter K of the Internal Revenue Code, a partnership functions as a flow-through conduit that does not pay federal income tax at the entity level; instead, partners report their pro-rata distributive shares of partnership income, deductions, and credits on their individual income tax returns.

PCS, Ltd., an Arizona limited partnership, was organized in 1981 by Edwin G. Hubert, who served as its general partner, with the stated purpose of developing and exploiting adaptations of an existing computer program called PRO-IV for use on various computer systems. Simultaneously upon its formation in 1981, PCS, Ltd. executed two interrelated contracts with an independent research firm, PCS, Inc., consisting of a Research and Development Agreement and a Technology Transfer Agreement. Under the Research and Development Agreement, PCS, Ltd. engaged PCS, Inc. as an independent contractor to perform the research and development work necessary to convert PRO-IV to run on IBM computers in exchange for cash and promissory notes, while retaining ownership of any resulting software; in total, the partnership invested $3,150,000 in the development of the program. Under the accompanying Technology Transfer Agreement, PCS, Ltd. granted PCS, Inc. the right to buy, for $5,000, an option on an exclusive and worldwide license to market any software resulting from the research effort, together with a 13-month review period in which PCS, Inc. could evaluate the software's marketing potential without interference by the partnership; PCS, Inc. could exercise the option by written notice before the end of that period, thereby obtaining the exclusive right to market the software and obligating itself to pay the partnership specified royalties on prospective sales. Based on its $3,150,000 contractual commitment, PCS, Ltd. claimed an immediate R&E deduction under I.R.C. § 174(a)(1) for the 1981 tax year, and the Kantors deducted their allocable share of the resulting partnership loss on their joint federal return.
The Tax Authority's Challenge

Following an examination of the partnership's activities, the Commissioner of Internal Revenue disallowed the Kantors' pass-through I.R.C. § 174 deduction in its entirety, determined a federal income tax deficiency for the 1981 taxable year, and assessed additions to tax for negligence under I.R.C. § 6653(a). The Internal Revenue Service (IRS) did not dispute that the partnership's expenditures were incurred for research and experimentation or that the enterprise was motivated by a genuine profit motive; instead, the Commissioner determined that PCS, Ltd. had not incurred the expenditures in connection with a trade or business of its own, as I.R.C. § 174 requires. As the Tax Court and the Ninth Circuit ultimately concluded, the simultaneously executed Research and Development Agreement and Technology Transfer Agreement—which delegated the development work to PCS, Inc. and gave it the right to obtain, for the nominal sum of $5,000, an option on an exclusive marketing license—showed that PCS, Ltd. was intended to be nothing more than an investment vehicle for a business that would be conducted by another entity, providing money in the hope of ultimately receiving royalties.

In addition to defending the substantive validity of the § 174 deduction before the United States Tax Court and on appeal to the Ninth Circuit, the Kantors raised—for the first time on appeal—a jurisdictional challenge under I.R.C. § 6212(a) and Scar v. Commissioner, 814 F.2d 1363 (9th Cir. 1987). The taxpayers asserted that the statutory Notice of Deficiency issued by the Commissioner was jurisdictionally invalid because the IRS had allegedly failed to make an individualized administrative "determination" of their tax liability prior to mailing the notice.
Governing Statutory Framework

The dispute in Kantor sits at the intersection of several foundational provisions of the Internal Revenue Code governing the capitalization, deduction, and crediting of research expenditures in the United States. During the tax year at issue (and prior to the mandatory amortization amendments enacted by the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 and subsequent statutory modifications under I.R.C. § 174A), I.R.C. § 174(a)(1) permitted a taxpayer to treat research or experimental expenditures paid or incurred during the taxable year "in connection with his trade or business" as expenses not chargeable to capital account, thereby allowing an immediate current deduction. Under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a), qualifying expenditures encompass research and development costs in the experimental or laboratory sense incident to the development or improvement of a product, including costs paid or incurred for research carried on in the taxpayer's behalf by another person or organization. Additionally, I.R.C. § 174(e) and Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(6) restrict eligibility to expenditures that are reasonable in amount under the circumstances.

Understanding the statutory mechanics of Kantor requires examining the historical interplay between I.R.C. § 162(a), § 195, and § 174(a)(1). Prior to the enactment of I.R.C. § 174 in 1954, taxpayers lacking an ongoing commercial business were forced to capitalize pre-operational research costs under the pre-opening expense doctrine. If the research effort produced an asset with a determinable useful life such as a patent, the start-up company could amortize the cost over that life, or deduct it as an abandonment loss if the project failed, but could not deduct the costs currently. While I.R.C. § 162(a) restricts ordinary and necessary business expense deductions to taxpayers actively "carrying on" an ongoing trade or business at the time the expense is incurred, Congress intentionally enacted the broader phrase "in connection with his trade or business" in I.R.C. § 174(a)(1). In the landmark decision Snow v. Commissioner, 416 U.S. 500 (1974), the United States Supreme Court resolved this statutory distinction by concluding that § 174 was intended to modify the restrictive "carrying on" standard of § 162 by providing new businesses, which are not yet selling goods or services, an immediate deduction for their research and experimental expenditures—making the deduction available, in the Ninth Circuit's later description, to "up-and-coming enterprises whose only 'business' at the time they incur research expenditures is the research itself".

Qualification under I.R.C. § 174 also serves as an absolute statutory gateway for claiming the federal Research and Development Tax Credit under I.R.C. § 41 (originally enacted as I.R.C. § 44F in the Economic Recovery Tax Act of 1981). Under I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(A), "qualified research" refers strictly to research with respect to which expenditures may be treated as specified research or experimental expenditures under § 174. Furthermore, I.R.C. § 41(b)(1) superimposes the narrower § 162 "carrying on" trade or business requirement onto qualified research expenses (QREs), and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e) (alongside the funded research exclusion of I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(H) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)) mandates that contract research expenses are eligible at the statutory 65% rate only if the research is performed "on behalf of" the taxpayer, the taxpayer bears the financial risk of failure, and the taxpayer retains "substantial rights" in the research results. Consequently, any entity that fails the threshold Kantor test under § 174 is automatically disqualified from claiming the § 41 R&D tax credit. Finally, on the procedural level, I.R.C. § 6212(a) provides that the Tax Court acquires subject matter jurisdiction only when the Commissioner makes a valid "determination" of a tax deficiency and issues a statutory Notice of Deficiency, while I.R.C. § 6653(a) (subsequently recodified into the accuracy-related penalty regime of I.R.C. § 6662) authorized an addition to tax if any part of an underpayment was attributable to negligence or intentional disregard of rules and regulations.
The Court's Final Holding

On July 20, 1993, a three-judge panel of the Ninth Circuit (Judges Hug, Fletcher, and Brunetti, with Judge Hug writing) affirmed in part and reversed in part: it affirmed the Tax Court on the substantive tax deficiency, held that the notice of deficiency was jurisdictionally valid (an issue the taxpayers raised for the first time on appeal), and reversed the imposition of negligence penalties. On the primary substantive issue, the Ninth Circuit affirmed the Tax Court's holding that PCS, Ltd. did not incur the $3,150,000 software research expenditures "in connection with" a trade or business of its own. Adopting the "Realistic Prospect" standard previously applied by the Fifth and Seventh Circuits, the Court held that while Snow permits start-up enterprises to deduct pre-operational research expenses, a taxpayer must demonstrate a "realistic prospect" of subsequently entering its own trade or business utilizing the technology if the research is successful. To establish this realistic prospect, the taxpayer must manifest both the objective intent to enter such a trade or business and the capability of doing so. Because PCS, Ltd. delegated the development work to an independent research firm, granted that firm the right to buy, for the nominal sum of $5,000, an option on an exclusive and worldwide marketing license, and appeared unlikely to have the resources to market the software itself, the Court concluded that PCS, Ltd. was intended to be nothing more than an investment vehicle for a business that would be conducted by PCS, Inc.

Regarding the procedural challenge, which the Court considered even though it was first raised on appeal because subject matter jurisdiction cannot be conferred by consent or waiver, the Ninth Circuit upheld the validity of the Notice of Deficiency and rejected the Kantors' jurisdictional argument under Scar, holding that judicial review of the Commissioner's internal administrative processes is barred unless the Notice of Deficiency reveals on its face that the IRS failed to make a determination specific to the taxpayer. Conversely, the Court reversed the negligence penalties imposed under I.R.C. § 6653(a). While recognizing that the assessment of a negligence penalty is presumptively correct (the taxpayer bearing the burden of proving the underpayment was not due to negligence) and that the Tax Court's penalty determination is reviewed for clear error, the Ninth Circuit concluded that when the Kantors subscribed to the partnership in 1981, the only case construing § 174 was the Supreme Court's 1974 decision, which did not squarely address the questions at issue, and that the post-Snow appellate jurisprudence delineating the exact boundary between a qualifying start-up venture and a passive R&D limited partnership had not yet crystallized—as Green v. Commissioner, 83 T.C. 667 (1984), Levin v. Commissioner, 832 F.2d 403 (7th Cir. 1987), and Spellman v. Commissioner, 845 F.2d 148 (7th Cir. 1988) were decided years later—and that general partner Hubert's experience and involvement with the PRO-IV project reasonably could have led investors to believe they were entitled to the deduction, with few, if any, warning signs, rendering the taxpayers' claiming of the deduction legally erroneous but not negligent.
(2) Core Legal & Evidentiary Failures

The disqualification of the claimed R&E deductions in Kantor—and the broader vulnerability of similar contract research structures under both I.R.C. § 174 and I.R.C. § 41—stemmed from five interconnected legal, contractual, operational, and evidentiary failures.
Contractual Divestiture of Commercialization Rights via the Nominally Priced $5,000 Option (Failure of Objective Intent)

The primary legal failure in Kantor was the contractual architecture erected between the partnership (PCS, Ltd.) and the research contractor (PCS, Inc.) at the inception of the venture. In evaluating whether a taxpayer possesses the requisite "objective intent" to enter a trade or business under I.R.C. § 174, courts look beyond self-serving recitations in offering memoranda or partnership agreements and examine the underlying economic reality and actual expectations of the parties at the time the agreements were executed. Simultaneously with the execution of the Research and Development Agreement, under which the partnership ultimately invested $3,150,000, PCS, Ltd. granted PCS, Inc. the right to buy, for just $5,000, an option on an exclusive and worldwide license to market any resulting software, exercisable upon written notice within a 13-month review period. From an economic standpoint, this nominally priced option created an asymmetric, one-way commercial trap: as the Ninth Circuit explained, by granting the research firm the right to purchase the option for a mere $5,000 and to exercise it upon written notice, the partnership rendered itself virtually incapable of becoming anything more than an investor.

The court found that this arrangement made it more probable than not that PCS, Inc. would purchase and exercise the option if the software resulting from the research was at all valuable. Upon exercise, PCS, Inc. would be entitled to market the program indefinitely on an exclusive and worldwide basis, and PCS, Ltd. would be totally prohibited from putting the program to any use whatsoever, relegating the partnership to the passive receipt of royalties on prospective sales. As established across multiple federal appellate circuits—including Spellman v. Commissioner, 845 F.2d 148 (7th Cir. 1988), Diamond v. Commissioner, 930 F.2d 372 (4th Cir. 1991), and Harris v. Commissioner, 16 F.3d 75 (5th Cir. 1994)—the receipt of royalties from an exclusive license granted at the outset of an endeavor constitutes passive investment income rather than the active conduct of a trade or business. Conversely, the court reasoned that if PCS, Inc. actually declined to purchase such a nominally priced option, it was unlikely that marketing the software would have been economically feasible. As the Ninth Circuit emphasized, "while the probability of a firm's going into its own business will satisfy section 174, the mere possibility of its doing so will not". Because the prospect that PCS, Ltd. might regain the marketing rights and market the software itself was a mere theoretical possibility rather than a probability—arising chiefly if the very company that built the software declined to pay a nominal $5,000 for the option—the agreements adequately supported the conclusion that the partnership planned to provide money and ultimately hoped to receive royalties, but did not anticipate developing or marketing the software itself.
Capital Depletion and Absence of Operational Infrastructure (Failure of Capability)

Even assuming arguendo that PCS, Inc. declined to purchase or exercise its nominally priced option, PCS, Ltd. independently failed the second prong of the Kantor test: the capability to enter the trade or business. The Ninth Circuit, relying on the record before the Tax Court, observed that it appeared unlikely that the partnership would have had the resources to market the software itself. According to the partnership's Private Placement Memorandum (PPM), PCS, Ltd. anticipated raising $3,500,000 and spending 90% of that sum on research activities alone, and it ultimately invested $3,150,000 in the development of the program. Just like the disqualified partnership in I-Tech R&D Limited Partnership v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2001-10 (aff'd sub nom. Lewin v. Commissioner, 335 F.3d 345 (4th Cir. 2003)), PCS, Ltd. lacked the capital to commercialize the software on its own: its PPM stated that if PCS, Inc. chose not to market the resulting program, the partnership would lack sufficient capital to market and license the program directly to consumers.

Furthermore, the development work was delegated entirely to PCS, Inc., whose programmers remained under that firm's sole and exclusive management and control rather than the partnership's. If PCS, Inc. walked away from the option, PCS, Ltd.—by its own PPM's admission—would have lacked sufficient capital to market and license the program directly to consumers, a speculative contingency that failed to demonstrate capability as of 1981, the tax year to which the court's inquiry was limited.
Independent Contractor Insulation and Investor-Level General Partner Involvement

To overcome these contractual and financial deficiencies, the Kantors argued that PCS, Ltd. actually engaged in the business of developing and marketing the software through the 1981 to 1987 activities of its general partner, Edwin G. Hubert. The Ninth Circuit, noting that its inquiry was limited to the 1981 tax year in which the deduction was claimed (so that Hubert's later activities were relevant only insofar as they indicated the partnership's intent and capability in 1981), analyzed both the legal language of the R&D Agreement and the substantive nature of Hubert's activities, finding both insufficient to attribute a trade or business to the partnership. The Research and Development Agreement between PCS, Ltd. and PCS, Inc. expressly stripped the partnership of operational authority, stipulating that "the full and exclusive relationship between them is that of an independent contractor and nothing in this Agreement shall be construed to create any relationship between the parties other than that of an independent contractor". Under this covenant, PCS, Inc. retained exclusive authority over the technical execution, engineering methodology, and personnel assigned to the software development.

The factual record showed that Hubert had over 12 years of sales and technical experience in the computer industry, had tested the PRO-IV software, and remained involved in the research effort—keeping in contact with the research firm's programmers, participating in strategic research decisions, reviewing research status reports, providing technical advice, and ultimately arranging a test site—yet the individuals developing the software were under the management and control of the research firm, an independent entity, not the partnership. The Ninth Circuit held that Hubert's identification of the technology, formation of the partnership, and negotiation of development and marketing agreements amounted to "the promotion and protection of a technological investment, not a business," and that his activities with the research firm were "consistent with those of any investor who applies his knowledge and expertise to insure that an investment is successful". Under federal tax law, monitoring a contractor to protect a prospective royalty stream or equity investment constitutes passive investment management rather than the active direction and control of a trade or business.
Cascading Disqualification Under I.R.C. § 41 (Formerly § 44F) Contract Research and Substantiation Rules

While Kantor was litigated directly over the threshold I.R.C. § 174 deduction, the Ninth Circuit subsequently applied Kantor to deny I.R.C. § 174 deductions claimed by investors in similarly structured R&D partnerships, notably in Gatto v. Commissioner, 1 F.3d 826 (9th Cir. 1993); neither decision adjudicated the research credit under I.R.C. § 44F (now I.R.C. § 41), so the credit analysis that follows extrapolates from their reasoning. From a technical R&D tax advisory perspective, the Kantor structure triggers a multi-layered disqualification under the federal R&D tax credit regime. First, because the expenditures failed to qualify as research or experimental expenditures incurred in connection with the taxpayer's trade or business under I.R.C. § 174, they are statutorily barred from entering the definition of "qualified research" under the gateway requirement of I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(A). Second, even where a pre-operational start-up satisfies the Kantor "realistic prospect" test for § 174 purposes (as later occurred in Scoggins v. Commissioner, 46 F.3d 950 (9th Cir. 1995)), I.R.C. § 41(b)(1) requires that qualified research expenses be paid or incurred in "carrying on" a trade or business (incorporating the strict I.R.C. § 162 standard), subject only to the narrow in-house research start-up exception of I.R.C. § 41(b)(4). An entity with no ongoing commercial operations and only contract research outlays cannot satisfy the general "carrying on" mandate of § 41(b)(1).

Third, the contractual structure in Kantor would, by extension, run afoul of the contract research "substantial rights" and "funded research" rules of I.R.C. § 41(b)(3), I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(H), Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e), and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d). Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e), a taxpayer may claim 65% of amounts paid or incurred to an outside contractor for qualified research only if the research is performed "on behalf of" the taxpayer, which requires that the taxpayer bear the financial risk of failure and retain "substantial rights" in the research results. Where, as with PCS, Ltd., a hiring entity grants the research contractor at inception the right to buy, for a nominal $5,000, an option on an exclusive worldwide license to the technology, the hiring entity has effectively positioned itself to surrender its substantial rights to the contractor whenever the research succeeds. Furthermore, from the perspective of the four-part test under I.R.C. § 41(d)—requiring a Permitted Purpose, Elimination of Uncertainty, a Process of Experimentation, and activities Technological in Nature—an entity that acts merely as a passive financial conduit without exercising technical direction, defining technical specifications, or documenting iterative hypothesis testing cannot substantiate that qualified research was conducted on its behalf.
Procedural Failure on the I.R.C. § 6212(a) Jurisdictional Challenge

On the procedural front, the Kantors' attempt to invalidate the statutory Notice of Deficiency under Scar v. Commissioner, 814 F.2d 1363 (9th Cir. 1987) failed due to an evidentiary misconception regarding the presumption of administrative regularity. In Scar, the IRS had issued a deficiency notice disallowing deductions arising from a mining tax shelter with which the taxpayers had no connection, and the attached documents indicated that, although the IRS knew the taxpayers had filed a return, the deficiency had been determined without examining it and computed using the maximum tax rate. The Kantors, raising the issue for the first time on appeal, argued that no actual determination had been made because the Commissioner did not determine until another year that PCS, Ltd. was not engaged in a trade or business; their only factual support was that the Commissioner had been forced to petition the Tax Court for an extension of time to answer their complaint, an argument the Ninth Circuit described as speculative at best. Relying on Clapp v. Commissioner, 875 F.2d 1396, 1402 (9th Cir. 1989), the Ninth Circuit held in Kantor that the Scar rule is strictly confined to instances where the Notice of Deficiency "reveals on its face that the Commissioner failed to make a determination". Because the Kantors' May 22, 1985 deficiency notice clearly indicated that their $12,500 PCS, Ltd. pass-through deduction was being disallowed, that their tax was being recomputed (yielding a $3,497 deficiency), and that a $174 negligence penalty was being imposed—with neither blatant error nor any statement suggesting that no determination had been made—the notice was facially valid, and the Court refused to "look behind a deficiency notice to question the Commissioner's motives and procedures leading to a [deficiency] determination".
(3) Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each statutory and judicial requirement addressed in Kantor v. Commissioner (and its companion Ninth Circuit precedent Scoggins v. Commissioner, 46 F.3d 950 (9th Cir. 1995)) against the specific factual and legal failures of PCS, Ltd. and the governing judicial standard of proof.

headers: Court's Standard of Proof & Judicial Benchmark

cells: Pre-Operational Trade or Business Nexus ("Realistic Prospect" Test) I.R.C. § 174(a)(1); Snow v. Commissioner, 416 U.S. 500 (1974)

PCS, Ltd. had no existing business and structured its contracts so that PCS, Inc. (the research contractor) would commercially exploit any successful software, leaving PCS, Ltd. as a passive royalty recipient.

A pre-operational taxpayer must prove a "realistic prospect"—defined as a probability, not a mere theoretical possibility—of subsequently entering its own trade or business utilizing the research results (assuming research success).
Prong 1: Objective Intent to Enter a Trade or Business I.R.C. § 174(a)(1); Kantor, 998 F.2d at 1518

Simultaneous execution of the R&D Agreement and Technology Transfer Agreement granted PCS, Inc. the right to buy, for a nominal $5,000, an option on an exclusive worldwide marketing license, against $3,150,000 of R&D spend. The court found this made it more probable than not that PCS, Inc. would purchase and exercise the option if the software was at all valuable.

Objective intent is determined by examining the economic reality and actual expectations of the parties at the time of contracting. The court set no pricing rule, but read together with later Ninth Circuit precedent, any contractor buy-out or licensing option should be priced at a substantial, fair-market exercise price (e.g., the $5 million purchase option—ten times the $500,000 research budget—exercisable only after a 15-month non-exclusive license and an 18-month partnership marketing period, upheld in Scoggins) or allow the taxpayer a meaningful window to market the technology independently.
Prong 2: Capability to Enter a Trade or Business I.R.C. § 174(a)(1); Kantor, 998 F.2d at 1518–20

PCS, Ltd.'s PPM anticipated spending 90% of the $3.5M it planned to raise on research alone (it invested $3.15M), leaving insufficient capital to market and license the program directly to consumers if PCS, Inc. chose not to market it, as the PPM itself acknowledged.

The taxpayer must demonstrate present financial, technical, and operational capability during the tax years at issue to exploit the research. This requires retained capital reserves for commercialization, access to distribution channels, or partners who personally possess the technical expertise and industry capability to direct commercialization.
Direction, Control, and Active Operational Involvement I.R.C. § 174(a)(1); Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a); Kantor, 998 F.2d at 1519–20

The R&D contract explicitly designated PCS, Inc. as an independent contractor with exclusive control. General Partner Edwin G. Hubert had over 12 years of computer-industry sales and technical experience and provided technical advice, but the programmers remained under the research firm's management and control; his activities were consistent with those of any investor who applies his knowledge and expertise to insure that an investment is successful.

Partner involvement must transcend passive investor oversight. Where research is contracted out, the Ninth Circuit held that the taxpayer must satisfy the trade or business requirement in some other way, such as by manufacturing or marketing the resulting technology; this showing is strongest where the taxpayer's principals are the actual inventors/technologists directing and guiding the development (as in Scoggins, where the partners personally invented the epitaxial reactor technology).
Contract Research "On Behalf Of" & Substantial Rights Retention I.R.C. § 41(b)(3); I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(H); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e)

Although PCS, Ltd. retained ownership of the software, by granting PCS, Inc. at the outset the right to buy, for $5,000, an option on an exclusive worldwide license, it rendered itself virtually incapable of becoming anything more than an investor (the court did not address § 41, but this structure bears directly on the substantial rights analysis).

For contract research to qualify under I.R.C. § 41 and § 174, the taxpayer must bear the financial risk of failure and retain substantial rights to exploit the research results without paying additional consideration or surrendering exclusive exploitation rights for nominal value at inception.
Facial Validity of Notice of Deficiency (Jurisdiction) I.R.C. § 6212(a); Scar v. Commissioner, 814 F.2d 1363 (9th Cir. 1987)

Raising the issue for the first time on appeal, the Kantors argued that no actual determination had been made because the Commissioner did not determine until another year that PCS, Ltd. lacked a trade or business, citing only the Commissioner's request for an extension of time to answer, despite the notice specifically disallowing their $12,500 PCS, Ltd. pass-through deduction for 1981.

Courts will not look behind a deficiency notice to examine the Commissioner's motives or internal administrative procedures unless the notice reveals on its face that the Commissioner failed to consider information relating to the specific taxpayer.
Negligence Penalty Rebuttal I.R.C. § 6653(a) (modern I.R.C. § 6662); Kantor, 998 F.2d at 1522
The IRS assessed negligence penalties against the Kantors for claiming the disallowed 1981 pass-through R&E deduction. (Taxpayer prevailed on this specific issue on appeal).

The Commissioner's negligence assessment is presumptively correct, the taxpayer bears the burden of proving the underpayment was not due to negligence, and the Tax Court's penalty determination is reviewed for clear error. However, the taxpayer rebuts negligence by demonstrating that claiming the deduction was reasonable at the time of investing (in 1981, post-Snow circuit boundaries on R&D partnerships were not yet established, and the general partner's experience and involvement could reasonably have led investors to believe they were entitled to the deduction, with few, if any, warning signs).

body.text: (4) Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To translate the appellate holdings of Kantor v. Commissioner—alongside its companion Ninth Circuit precedent Scoggins v. Commissioner, 46 F.3d 950 (9th Cir. 1995), I.R.C. § 174/§ 174A, and I.R.C. § 41—into actionable tax practice, the following two industry case studies examine modern United States research ventures initially structured with the exact fatal flaws identified in Kantor. Each case study demonstrates step-by-step how the taxpayer can restructure its project governance, contract terms, technical documentation, and experimentation tracking to overcome judicial scrutiny and establish full eligibility for R&D tax benefits.
Case Study 1: Enterprise Cloud & Autonomous AI Software Venture (Pre-Operational Joint Venture Contracting with an External Software Development Firm)
Baseline Fact Pattern and Identification of Kantor Pitfalls

Aegis FinTech Ventures, LLC ("Aegis LLC"), a Delaware limited liability company taxed as a partnership under Subchapter K, is formed by a syndicate of high-net-worth financial executives and angel investors in San Francisco, California, within the appellate jurisdiction of the Ninth Circuit. Aegis LLC raises $4,500,000 in partner capital to develop a novel, low-latency cryptographic fraud-detection and autonomous neural-network routing engine for institutional payment rails. Under its initial, defective legal structure, Aegis LLC commits $4,400,000 of its $4,500,000 capital to VectorCode Labs, Inc. ("VectorCode"), an established software engineering corporation, under a Turnkey Software Development Agreement. That agreement stipulates that VectorCode acts solely as an independent contractor with exclusive control over software architecture and coding. Simultaneously, Aegis LLC and VectorCode execute a Commercialization Option Agreement granting VectorCode an irrevocable option to acquire an exclusive, worldwide, perpetual license to market and SaaS-host the resulting software engine for a flat exercise fee of $10,000, plus a 7% royalty on net revenues. Aegis LLC has no employees, retains only $100,000 for administrative legal and accounting fees, and relies on its managing member—a retired investment banker with no computer science credentials—to attend monthly 30-minute status calls with VectorCode. Aegis LLC intends to claim the $4,400,000 outlay as domestic R&E expenditures under I.R.C. § 174/§ 174A and claim the I.R.C. § 41 R&D tax credit.

Under Kantor, this baseline structure faces certain disallowance upon IRS examination. First, the $10,000 option strike price against $4,400,000 of R&D funding replicates the right PCS, Ltd. gave its research firm to buy, for a nominal $5,000, an option on an exclusive license to software developed with $3,150,000 of R&D funding in Kantor, undermining objective intent because, as in that case, it makes it more probable than not that VectorCode will exercise the option if the AI fraud engine is at all valuable, relegating Aegis LLC to passive royalty collection. Second, by committing 97.8% of its capital ($4,400,000 of $4,500,000) to the turnkey R&D fee, Aegis LLC fails the capability prong because it lacks the financial reserves, cloud infrastructure, or sales personnel to deploy or license an enterprise SaaS product if VectorCode declines the option. Third, the managing member's monthly status calls represent passive investor monitoring rather than active business direction, while the $10,000 exclusive buy-out option surrenders "substantial rights" under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e) and fails the "carrying on" requirement of I.R.C. § 41(b)(1).
Step 1: Restructuring Project Governance and Operational Capability

To rehabilitate Aegis LLC before executing contracts or incurring expenditures, the venture must first reconstitute its management and financial reserves to mirror the taxpayer structure upheld by the Ninth Circuit in Scoggins v. Commissioner, 46 F.3d 950 (9th Cir. 1995). In Scoggins, the Ninth Circuit reversed the Tax Court and allowed § 174 deductions in significant part because the partnership was composed of the actual technologists who invented the reactor technology and possessed the personal capability to guide its development and commercialization. Accordingly, Aegis LLC must admit two veteran principal distributed-systems architects—the actual conceivers of the initial cryptographic fraud algorithm—as Managing Technical Members holding meaningful equity and operational governance authority.

Simultaneously, rather than exhausting 97.8% of partnership capital on the R&D contract, Aegis LLC must restructure its $4,500,000 capitalization (or raise an additional $1,500,000 financing tranche) so that no more than $3,200,000 is allocated to Phase I contract R&D, while $1,300,000 is segregated in an irrevocable Commercialization and Go-To-Market Reserve. Formal board resolutions and the Amended Operating Agreement must legally restrict this $1,300,000 reserve to funding direct SaaS cloud hosting, SOC-2 security compliance, enterprise sales engineering, and direct customer acquisition by Aegis LLC. Furthermore, to bridge the statutory gap between I.R.C. § 174 ("in connection with") and I.R.C. § 41(b)(1) ("carrying on"), Aegis LLC must directly employ the two Lead Systems Architects as W-2 employees performing in-house core algorithm design and actively execute beta-testing pilot agreements with regional financial institutions, thereby establishing both an active trade or business and qualification under the in-house start-up credit provisions of I.R.C. § 41(b)(4).
Step 2: Re-Engineering Contract Terms, Option Pricing, and IP Allocation

The second remedial step requires completely dismantling the nominal $10,000 exclusive worldwide licensing option and replacing it with a Scoggins-compliant commercialization framework. Under the revised Master Services and Technology Agreement, Aegis LLC must retain 100% unencumbered legal and beneficial title, patents, copyrights, and trade secrets in all source code, neural-network training weights, and technical documentation developed under the contract. To preserve Aegis LLC's realistic prospect of entering its own software business, the contract must establish a mandatory 18-to-24 month independent marketing window following R&D completion during which Aegis LLC holds the immediate, unencumbered right to market, license, and deploy the SaaS platform directly to financial institutions. During this window, VectorCode may be granted, at most, a limited, non-exclusive license restricted to a non-competing industry vertical (such as healthcare claims auditing), leaving Aegis LLC free to exploit the core banking market.

If VectorCode insists upon an option to acquire broader commercialization rights in the future, the option cannot become exercisable until at least 24 months after prototype completion, and the option strike price must be fixed at a substantial, arm's-length valuation that significantly exceeds the R&D investment—specifically, $12,000,000, representing nearly four times the $3,200,000 R&D budget and following the principle of the $5,000,000 purchase option (ten times the partnership's $500,000 research budget) upheld in Scoggins. This substantial exercise price flips the economic reality analyzed in Kantor: VectorCode will only exercise the option if the software achieves extraordinary commercial value, and even then only after Aegis LLC has operated its own SaaS licensing business for two years. Finally, the Master Services Agreement must eliminate boilerplate independent contractor insulation and expressly mandate that VectorCode performs coding tasks strictly "on behalf of" Aegis LLC under the direct architectural supervision, sprint specification, and acceptance-testing criteria dictated by Aegis LLC's Managing Technical Members, while structuring payments on a time-and-materials or milestone-contingent basis so that Aegis LLC bears the financial risk of technical failure under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e).
Step 3: Technical Direction and Process of Experimentation Tracking

To satisfy both the Kantor realistic-prospect analysis (in which the general partner's technical advice proved insufficient because the programmers remained under the research firm's control) and the four-part test of I.R.C. § 41(d), Aegis LLC must institute rigorous technical governance over VectorCode's engineering work. Prior to commencing coding, Aegis LLC's Managing Technical Members must author a formal Technical Design Document (TDD) defining the exact capability and architectural uncertainties under I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(A) and Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)—specifically detailing why existing deterministic rule engines and standard transformer architectures cannot achieve sub-15-millisecond inference latency under encrypted homomorphic data payloads without exceeding a 0.01% false-positive rate. Throughout execution, Aegis LLC's in-house architects must maintain administrative control over the Git/GitHub code repository, define the bi-weekly agile sprint hypotheses, and issue formal engineering directives to VectorCode's developers. For each sprint, Aegis LLC's tracking system must record the mathematical or algorithmic hypothesis formulated by Aegis LLC's architects, the simulation or benchmark test executed by VectorCode within Aegis LLC's testing harness, the quantitative latency and throughput test results, and Aegis LLC's technical sign-off or architectural pivot directive whenever an iteration fails to meet target metrics.
Step 4: Contemporaneous Documentation and Substantiation Protocols

To build an audit-ready evidentiary record that defeats any IRS challenge under Kantor or I.R.C. § 6001, Aegis LLC must maintain a contemporaneous Intent and Capability Dossier compiled prior to contract execution. This dossier must preserve board minutes, an independent third-party valuation report justifying the $12,000,000 option strike price, bank escrow statements proving the segregated $1,300,000 Commercialization Reserve, and executed letters of intent from prospective banking pilot customers. Alongside financial records, Aegis LLC must archive weekly technical steering committee minutes and pull-request review logs signed by its Managing Technical Members demonstrating active rejection, modification, and direction of VectorCode's code commits—proving that Aegis LLC's involvement far exceeds the investor-level involvement found insufficient in Kantor and Lewin. Finally, VectorCode must be contractually required to submit itemized monthly invoices mapped directly to specific R&D sprint tickets and technical uncertainties, enabling Aegis LLC's tax advisors to segregate qualifying experimental software engineering (eligible at 65% under I.R.C. § 41(b)(3)) from routine user-interface formatting or administrative maintenance.
Case Study 2: Semiconductor & Advanced Robotics Hardware Spin-Out (Corporate-Sponsored R&D Partnership with Affiliate Buy-Out Trap)
Baseline Fact Pattern and Identification of Kantor Pitfalls

FabLogic Systems, Inc. ("FabLogic"), an established United States semiconductor equipment manufacturer, seeks off-balance-sheet financing to develop a next-generation atomic-layer deposition (ALD) robotic wafer-handling chamber. FabLogic's executives and tax promoters form a separate limited partnership, Precision Wafer R&D Partners, LP ("Precision LP"), raising $8,000,000 from outside passive limited partners. FabLogic's corporate Vice President of Finance serves as the administrative General Partner of Precision LP. Under the initial transaction documents, Precision LP licenses baseline background patents from FabLogic, pays FabLogic $7,950,000 under an Exclusive R&D Agreement to design and build the ALD robotic prototype inside FabLogic's cleanroom facilities using FabLogic's staff engineers, and grants FabLogic a nominal $2,500 option to acquire all rights, title, and exclusive manufacturing licenses to the resulting ALD chamber technology upon completion in exchange for a 4% sales royalty. Furthermore, under the Development Agreement, FabLogic is designated as Precision LP's exclusive agent with sole power to file regulatory approvals and patent applications in FabLogic's own corporate name. Precision LP retains only $50,000 in cash, leases no cleanroom or manufacturing space, employs no engineers, and claims a $7,950,000 R&E deduction/amortization base under I.R.C. § 174 alongside I.R.C. § 41 contract research tax credits.

This baseline structure violates multiple core tenets of Kantor and companion federal circuit decisions. As the Ninth Circuit held in Kantor, 998 F.2d at 1519, "a taxpayer's existing or prospective business must be its own and not that of another entity". Precision LP is structured purely as a financing conduit to expand FabLogic's existing semiconductor equipment business, mirroring the disqualified structures in Levin v. Commissioner, 832 F.2d 403 (7th Cir. 1987), Diamond v. Commissioner, 930 F.2d 372 (4th Cir. 1991), and IRS Chief Counsel Advice 200145011. The $2,500 buy-out option replicates the fatal nominal options in Kantor (the nominal $5,000 price to purchase an option on an exclusive license) and Diamond (where the contractor held contractual control over research, production, marketing, and licensing of the robotics technology), making it more probable than not that FabLogic will monopolize any successful ALD robotics technology. Moreover, even if FabLogic declined the option, Precision LP possesses only $50,000 in working capital and lacks the multi-million-dollar cleanroom facilities required to complete development or manufacture ALD wafer chambers, failing the capability prong due to the prohibitive cost of independent market entry.
Step 1: Restructuring Entity Governance and Operational Substance

To transform this defective tax-shelter arrangement into a legally compliant, substantive joint research and commercialization venture capable of claiming I.R.C. § 174 and I.R.C. § 41 benefits, Precision LP must be restructured into an active operating Joint Venture LLC ("Precision ALD Technologies, LLC") co-managed by the lead physicists and mechanical engineers who are transferred or seconded directly into the venture. The Managing Board of Precision ALD Technologies, LLC must consist of active semiconductor technologists owing independent fiduciary duties to the joint venture, thereby eliminating the fatal conflict of interest wherein a financial officer of the research contractor serves as the sole general partner.

To establish financial and operational capability during the tax years at issue, Precision ALD Technologies, LLC must reallocate its $8,000,000 capitalization so that $5,500,000 funds the R&D phase while $2,500,000 is retained in a dedicated working capital reserve to fund post-prototype commercial production and sales. Because constructing a proprietary semiconductor cleanroom from scratch is capital-prohibitive, Precision ALD Technologies, LLC must establish present operational capability under Kantor by executing binding Commercial Foundry and Contract Manufacturing Agreements with third-party cleanroom fabricators (or a binding, arm's-length toll-manufacturing agreement with FabLogic whereby FabLogic fabricates chambers strictly as a contract manufacturer for Precision ALD Technologies, LLC to sell under Precision's own brand to third-party chipmakers). As recognized in IRS Field Service Advice (POSTF-127347-05) and Scoggins, a research entity need not own physical manufacturing plants, office equipment, or telephones during the R&D phase so long as its capital reserves and contractual arrangements give it the realistic operational capability to commercialize the resulting product for its own account once development concludes.
Step 2: Re-Engineering Contract Terms, Licensing, and Buy-Out Mechanics

The second remedial step requires reversing the defective agency and intellectual property clauses criticized in IRS CCA 200145011, together with the nominally priced option structure rejected in Kantor. Under the restructured Development Agreement, all patent applications, cleanroom safety certifications, and technical schematics generated during the ALD project must be filed directly in the name of, and owned 100% by, Precision ALD Technologies, LLC. The nominal $2,500 exclusive buy-out option must be eliminated in favor of a two-track commercialization structure that preserves Precision ALD Technologies, LLC's realistic prospect of conducting its own trade or business. Under the first track, upon completion of the ALD robotic prototype, Precision ALD Technologies, LLC retains the unrestricted right to sell ALD chambers directly to global semiconductor foundries via its toll-manufacturing contracts, or to engage in an active business of non-exclusively licensing the ALD technology to multiple competing semiconductor equipment OEMs.

Under the second track, if FabLogic is granted an option to acquire exclusive rights to the ALD technology, the option must be subject to an initial 18-to-24 month period during which Precision ALD Technologies, LLC holds exclusive exploitation rights (or during which FabLogic holds only a non-exclusive license), coupled with a substantial option exercise price set at independent Fair Market Value or a fixed strike price of at least $20,000,000 (nearly four times the $5,500,000 R&D expenditure). Under Kantor and Scoggins, a high exercise price removes the near-certainty of contractor exercise that a nominal price creates, making it probable and realistic that Precision ALD Technologies, LLC will commercially exploit the technology itself unless FabLogic pays a massive commercial premium. Additionally, to comply with I.R.C. § 41(b)(3) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e), the R&D Engineering Services Agreement must structure payments to FabLogic's cleanroom engineering team based on experimental research milestones rather than guaranteed turnkey product delivery—placing the financial risk of technical failure squarely on Precision ALD Technologies, LLC—while explicitly confirming that Precision ALD Technologies, LLC retains all substantial rights to the resulting ALD designs without paying any further fee or royalty.
Step 3: Technical Direction and Process of Experimentation Tracking

To substantiate that Precision ALD Technologies, LLC is actively directing hardware experimentation rather than passively funding FabLogic's internal R&D pipeline, Precision ALD Technologies, LLC's technical principals must author the baseline Engineering Requirements Specification (ERS) detailing the physical and thermodynamic uncertainties under I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)—such as eliminating particulate contamination and thermal deformation in robotic end-effectors operating inside a vacuum plasma deposition chamber. Throughout the prototype build under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a) (pilot models) and I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(C), Precision ALD Technologies, LLC's lead engineers must direct and approve each phase of the experimental process. This technical governance encompasses directing Finite Element Analysis (FEA) thermal and fluid-dynamics simulations evaluating candidate ceramic-composite robotic arm geometries, issuing formal Fabrication Authorization Orders signed by Precision's technical director to machine experimental prototype sub-assemblies, and evaluating cleanroom vacuum-chamber test logs recording wafer-alignment variance, thermal drift failures, and iterative mechanical redesigns.
Step 4: Contemporaneous Documentation and Substantiation Protocols

To insulate the restructured hardware venture against IRS disallowance under Kantor, Diamond, and I-Tech, Precision ALD Technologies, LLC must implement a comprehensive documentation matrix mapping contemporaneous artifacts directly to each judicial requirement:

cells: Objective Intent Substantiation

Executed Joint Venture Operating Agreement; Independent Valuation Report supporting the $20M option strike price; Pre-development marketing plans and direct customer outreach logs to third-party chip foundries.

Defeats the Kantor "nominal option" inference (the court found a nominally priced option made exercise more probable than not) by proving the parties objectively expected Precision ALD Technologies, LLC to commercialize the hardware unless a massive FMV buyout was paid.
Capability Substantiation
Bank escrow statements verifying the segregated $2.5M Commercialization Reserve; Executed Toll-Manufacturing Letter of Intent; CVs and employment agreements of Precision's technical principals.
Satisfies the Kantor and Scoggins capability prong by demonstrating present financial and operational capacity to produce and market the ALD chambers during the tax years under audit.
Direction & Control Substantiation
Bi-weekly Engineering Change Orders (ECOs), CAD approval sign-offs, and cleanroom test failure directives authored by Precision's technical managers directing the contract engineers.
Proves active entrepreneurial direction and control rather than the investor-level involvement found insufficient in Kantor and Lewin.
I.R.C. § 174 / § 41 Project & Cost Accounting

Project-level general ledger sub-accounts segregating direct prototype materials, W-2 technical supervision wages, and 65% qualifying contract research invoices tied to specific FEA/prototype test iterations.
Satisfies I.R.C. § 174(e) reasonableness, Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e) contract research rules, and strict substantiation standards for the four-part test under I.R.C. § 41(d).

body.text: (5) Synthesis & Strategic Conclusions for U.S. Tax Practitioners

The Ninth Circuit's decision in Kantor v. Commissioner remains a foundational pillar of United States R&D tax jurisprudence because it permanently closed the structural loophole that tax shelter syndicators attempted to wedge open following Snow v. Commissioner. While Snow established that an up-and-coming enterprise need not currently be selling goods or services to claim research and experimental deductions under I.R.C. § 174, Kantor adopted the rigorous Realistic Prospect Test applied by the Fifth and Seventh Circuits—holding that it requires objective proof of both the intent and the capability to enter the taxpayer's own trade or business—to separate genuine entrepreneurial innovation from passive capital syndication.

For corporate tax directors, R&D tax credit attorneys, and venture structuring advisors operating in the United States, Kantor establishes three enduring operational imperatives. First, substance governs over form in licensing and buy-out options: whenever a research entity outsources development to a contractor and simultaneously grants that contractor an option to license or acquire the resulting intellectual property, the IRS and federal courts will scrutinize the option strike price relative to the R&D budget, and a nominally priced option—like the $5,000 option price in that case, which the court found made exercise more probable than not—will defeat the "realistic prospect" required under I.R.C. § 174 and, by extension, jeopardize the retention of "substantial rights" required under I.R.C. § 41. Second, pre-revenue entities must maintain dedicated capital and operational reserves: an entity that exhausts virtually all of its committed capital on contract R&D fees while retaining no financial reserves, personnel, or contractual manufacturing and distribution pathways to commercialize the resulting technology will fail the Kantor capability prong, as the Ninth Circuit's affirmance of the Tax Court's findings illustrates. Finally, active technical governance must replace investor-level oversight: contractual boilerplate declaring the research performer an autonomous independent contractor, combined with general partner involvement that—like Hubert's technical advice and participation in strategic research decisions—leaves the contractor's personnel under the contractor's control, reduces the funding entity to a mere investor. Only when the taxpayer's own principals possess technical competence, actively direct the process of experimentation, retain unencumbered commercial exploitation rights, and maintain the financial capability to bring the technology to market will the expenditures survive judicial scrutiny under I.R.C. § 174 and I.R.C. § 41.

metaDescription: Kantor v. Commissioner (9th Cir. 1993): contract research is deductible under IRC § 174 only with a realistic prospect of entering one's own business.
